comments.author: @AlexBradburn2025
comments.text:
Long before the world discovered Seychelles as a paradise of crystal waters, granite mountains and white beaches, these islands became home to a people and a culture that slowly grew from many different roots.
Seychelles was never built by one race alone. Africans, Europeans, Indians, Chinese and people from many parts of the world contributed to the society that became Seychellois. From that mixture came something unique — the Seychellois identity.
But today, many Seychellois are asking an uncomfortable question:
What happens when the people who were born on these islands begin to feel like strangers in their own homeland?
Over the years, more expatriates have arrived in Seychelles to work, invest, establish businesses and settle. Immigration itself is not necessarily the problem. Seychelles has always welcomed people from different backgrounds.
The concern begins when economic growth and migration move faster than the ability of the country to protect its people, culture, housing, land, employment opportunities and national identity.
A small island has limited land and limited resources. When the population grows, the pressure is felt everywhere — in housing prices, employment, traffic, businesses, public services and access to land.
And there is another concern that deserves a serious conversation:
Our history must never be rewritten.
People who come to Seychelles today may have family connections to the islands, may have ancestors who lived here, or may have contributed greatly to the country. Those contributions should be acknowledged.
But claiming historical ownership of Seychelles or suggesting that one particular community alone represents the country's original roots ignores the complicated history that created the Seychellois nation.
Seychelles belongs to its citizens.
Not because of the colour of their skin.
Not because of their ancestry.
But because generations of Seychellois built their lives, families, communities and future here.
Being Seychellois means protecting the culture, respecting the Creole heritage, understanding the history and making sure that development benefits the people who call these islands home.
We should not hate the foreigner.
We should not attack someone because of where they were born.
But neither should we be afraid to speak when we feel that our homeland is changing faster than we can understand.
A country can welcome the world without losing itself.
Seychelles can remain open, multicultural and prosperous while still saying:
Respect our history. Respect our culture. Respect our people.
Because paradise is not only the beaches, mountains and ocean.
Paradise is also the people who call it home.
And if we want future generations of Seychellois to know what it truly means to belong to these islands, then we must protect our identity today — peacefully, proudly and responsibly.
